scenes.title: Looking for 72 the slow way
scenes.narration: Say you want to find seventy two in this list.

steps.say: If you do not know the list is in order, all you can do is check every box, starting from the first.
Is it two? No.
Is it five? No.
Eight? No.
And so on, until the eleventh box finally holds seventy two.
If the number sits at the very end, or is not there at all, you check all sixteen.
We can do much better, if the list is sorted. That one rule is the whole trick.

scenes.title: Two pointers and a midpoint
scenes.narration: Instead of starting at the front, put one pointer at each end.

steps.say: L marks the start, at index zero. R marks the end, at index fifteen.
Halfway between them is index seven.
It holds forty five. Now ask one question. Is seventy two equal to it, smaller, or bigger?
Why not add L and R and halve that? On a huge list, the sum can overflow in Java or C.
Taking half the gap from L never gets that big.

scenes.title: One look rules out half
scenes.narration: Here is where the order pays off.

steps.say: The target is bigger than forty five.
Every box left of it is even smaller. So none of those first eight can be the one.
We cross them all out in one go, and L jumps to index eight.
Find the new middle. It is index eleven.
It holds seventy nine. The target is smaller.
So index eleven and everything right of it are out. R moves to index ten.
Sixteen boxes went down to half, and now just three are left, after only two looks.

scenes.title: Closing in on 72
scenes.narration: Three boxes are left: fifty six, sixty seven and seventy two.

steps.say: The middle is index nine.
It holds sixty seven, which is too small.
So L moves past it, to index ten.
Now L and R meet, and the middle is index ten.
It holds seventy two. Found, on the fourth look.

scenes.title: Each look leaves half or less
scenes.narration: Line up what was still in play before each look.

steps.say: Sixteen boxes before the first look.
Half of them before the second.
Three before the third. Each look also throws out the middle box.
And one box for the last look.
Sixteen, eight, three, one. Every look halves what is left. Halve n about log two of n times, and one box is left.

draw.write: n halved k times = 1, so k = log₂ n

steps.say: So doubling the list adds just one more look.

scenes.narration: Here is the most looks it can ever take, as the list grows.

steps.say: Sixteen boxes take at most five looks. Our search got lucky and needed four.
A thousand take at most ten, and a million at most twenty.
And four billion take at most thirty two.
Checking one by one, the worst case is a check for every box. That bar would run millions of times off the board.
